version.changelog:
Initial release of qwenspeak: text-to-speech over SSH with secure, containerized Qwen3-TTS.

- Generate speech using preset voices, voice design, or voice cloning.
- File operations (upload, download, directory management) via SSH with strict path isolation.
- Required: Configure SSH access and environment variables (`QWENSPEAK_HOST`, `QWENSPEAK_PORT`).
- Secure command execution—no shell access, all operations whitelisted in a Python wrapper.
- Includes detailed usage examples for TTS generation and file management.

llm.summary: The skill's stated purpose (SSH-based TTS) is plausible, but the instructions omit and mismatch important operational details (ssh client requirement, port, and authentication), and they implicitly require access to the user's SSH keys/known_hosts and file upload/download — these gaps make the package incoherent and worth caution before installing.

dimensions.detail: The name and description (Qwen3-TTS over an SSH-locked container) match the runtime instructions to run SSH commands against a tts user. Requesting a host (QWENSPEAK_HOST) is consistent. However the metadata declares only QWENSPEAK_HOST as the primaryEnv while the SKILL.md explicitly requires QWENSPEAK_PORT as well — a mismatch that could break or hide needed configuration.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: The SKILL.md instructs the agent/user to run SSH commands (ssh -p $QWENSPEAK_PORT tts@$QWENSPEAK_HOST "...") and to accept the host key (which writes to ~/.ssh/known_hosts). It also describes file upload/download commands (put/get) that transfer user data to/from the remote container. The instructions do not declare or constrain how SSH authentication occurs (ssh keys, agent, or password), so in practice the skill will rely on the user's SSH keys/agent/credentials — a privacy/security surface not documented or requested explicitly.

dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: No install spec and no code files are present; the skill is instruction-only so it does not install third-party code on disk. This is the lowest-risk install model.

dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: Declared primary credential is QWENSPEAK_HOST, but the skill also needs QWENSPEAK_PORT and implicitly SSH authentication material. The registry metadata lists no required env vars despite SKILL.md requiring both host and port. The skill does not request or document any SSH key variables (e.g., a dedicated SSH_PRIVATE_KEY) yet will rely on the user's SSH client and keys — an under-declared, disproportionate implicit dependency on sensitive credentials.

dimensions.detail: always:false and model invocation allowed — normal. The SKILL.md asks users to add env config to ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json (reasonable) and to accept the host key into ~/.ssh/known_hosts (will persist a fingerprint). Those are typical for SSH-based integrations but should be noted because they modify user files outside the skill's own sandbox.

llm.guidance:
This skill uses SSH to run TTS commands on a remote container — that means:

- Confirm you trust the remote host/container before connecting. The skill instructs you to accept its SSH host key (which will be written to ~/.ssh/known_hosts).
- The SKILL.md omits or mismatches important details: it requires QWENSPEAK_PORT but the registry metadata only lists QWENSPEAK_HOST; the skill also implicitly depends on an SSH client and your SSH authentication (private keys or agent), but it doesn't declare or ask for those credentials explicitly. Expect the agent to use whatever SSH keys are available in your environment.
- Because put/get transfer files to/from the remote container, avoid uploading sensitive audio or secrets. If you need to use voice-clone features, consider using throwaway/dedicated SSH keys and an isolated environment.
- Before installing, verify the upstream project (https://github.com/psyb0t/docker-qwenspeak), review the container/server code, and, if possible, run the server in a controlled VM or sandbox. If you proceed, prefer a dedicated SSH key with limited scope and avoid reusing keys that grant broader access.

Given the missing declarations and implicit access to your SSH credentials/files, proceed cautiously — these are design/description mismatches rather than definitive proof of malice.
